summary: Examines address resolution problems that appear when data centers grow to very large numbers of hosts. It focuses on ARP for IPv4 and Neighbor Discovery for IPv6, and describes the scaling issues they can cause. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If thousands of people in a huge hall all shout who has this name to find a friend, it gets noisy. This describes that noise problem in giant computer rooms.

questions: why does arp not scale in large data centers
what are neighbor discovery problems in data centers
how does neighbor discovery differ from arp
subtitle: Why ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery become a burden when data centers grow to huge numbers of hosts and virtual machines.

tldr.problem: Virtualization and workload mobility push data centers toward very large Layer 2 networks, where address resolution traffic from ARP in IPv4 and Neighbor Discovery in IPv6 can overload routers and switches.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a generalized three-layer data center design, shows how different Layer 2 and Layer 3 placements change the load, and itemizes specific pain points on routers and switches.
tldr.outcome: It only lists problems and does not propose solutions. The authors hope that describing the pain points will start a discussion of whether and how to address them.

facts.value: low thousands of packets per second

today: RFC 6820 is an Informational document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records problems and proposes no solutions, leaving the discussion of whether and how to address them to others.

sections.title: Scope: Address Resolution in Big Data Centers
sections.content:
This memo examines scaling issues in large data centers, focusing on address resolution: finding the link-layer address that matches an IP address. IPv4 does this with ARP and IPv6 with Neighbor Discovery (ND).

Strictly, address resolution stays inside one Layer 2 broadcast domain. But routers with many interfaces, and IEEE 802.1Q networks where each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, spread the effect across both links and devices. The scope mirrors the charter of the Address Resolution for Massive numbers of hosts in the Data center (ARMD) working group, and the document lists current pain points without covering broader data center issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is about one chore: figuring out which mailbox belongs to which address. It asks what happens to that chore when there are a gigantic number of mailboxes.

sections.title: Why Layer 2 Networks Keep Growing
sections.content:
Large flat Layer 2 networks have long had scaling problems: more broadcast traffic from protocols like ARP, which every switch, host and router must process, and in extreme cases broadcast storms that bring down part or all of a network. The conventional answer was to split them into smaller subnets, for example one IP subnet per rack, confining the broadcast domain to one top-of-rack (ToR) switch.

That conflicts with server virtualization and dynamic workload placement. A virtual machine is easiest to move when its IP address does not have to change, which favors one big Layer 2 network. A single physical server may host ten or more VMs, each with its own IP and MAC address. The memo notes data centers with over 100,000 physical machines and many times that number of VMs, and says the issues might appear at any scale depending on design.
sections.plainLanguage: It used to be tidy to keep each class in its own room. But when kids keep moving between classes, schools want one giant room, and shouting names across it gets loud.

sections.title: ARP Versus Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
In IPv4 over Ethernet, a node broadcasts an ARP Request to the whole Layer 2 network, and the owner of the address sends an ARP Reply. The memo calls ARP old and sparsely documented: there are no clear requirements for retransmitting requests, so implementations vary. Its scaling problems are broadcast volume, host implementations that are too entrenched to change, and no clear guidance on flushing stale entries, so some implementations flush caches every few minutes and send new queries. Changes may be possible in hypervisors, boundary routers or ToR switches, for example Proxy ARP.

IPv6 ND works much like ARP, but uses multicast instead of broadcast. A query for a target address is mapped to a Solicited Node multicast address, so most nodes filter out the unwanted query in the network card rather than in host software. Where that filtering cannot be done in hardware, such as on hypervisors, it must be done in software such as the vSwitch.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP is like yelling a name to the whole room. ND is like whispering only to the small group who might know, so most people never have to listen.

sections.title: A Generalized Data Center Design
sections.content:
The memo abstracts most data centers into three layers: the access layer of switches closest to the servers (usually ToR, sometimes End-of-Row), the aggregation layer that interconnects many access switches, and the Core that connects aggregation to the wider network. Aggregation switches interconnecting hundreds of ToR switches are described as no longer uncommon.

Where the Layer 3 boundary sits changes the ARP and ND load. With L3 to the access switches, each rack is its own L2 domain and there are no significant scaling issues, but VMs cannot move between racks. With L3 to the aggregation switches, VMs can migrate without address changes, but all VLANs on all access ports act like one big L2 domain and the aggregation switches carry a significant ARP and ND load. With L3 in the core only, VLANs span more racks, giving the largest ARP and ND impact. Overlays can redefine where the boundary sits but do not remove address resolution traffic, they just move it into regular data traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a school with classrooms, floors and a front office. Where you put the front office desk decides how many questions pile up at it.

sections.title: The Itemized Pain Points
sections.content:
ARP processing on routers. Routers often handle ARP in a software slow path, supporting ARP in the low thousands of packets per second, far below what forwarding hardware manages. Mitigations include discarding ARP Requests for addresses not owned by the router and broadcasting periodic gratuitous ARPs so neighbors refresh entries. Packets with no ARP entry are queued while resolution runs, which can be CPU intensive, and routers with 100 or more interfaces face the aggregate load.

IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. ND requires nodes to revalidate in-use entries, and some implementations probe as often as every 35 seconds. The gratuitous ARP trick does not work in IPv6, because gratuitous ND updates cannot mark an entry valid. Running IPv4 and IPv6 together compounds both sets of issues.

MAC address tables. Switches learn source addresses from flooded broadcast, multicast and unknown-destination frames, and each VM adds its own MAC address, so table size becomes a problem as the L2 domain grows, especially when L3 stops at the aggregation switches.
sections.plainLanguage: The main desk can only answer so many questions a second. When more kids ask, and keep re-checking old answers, the line grows and the address book fills up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that it creates no security implications and has none. It notes that the security vulnerabilities in ARP are well known and that this document neither changes nor mitigates them. Security considerations for Neighbor Discovery are discussed in RFC 4861 and RFC 6583.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo only describes a problem, so it adds no new safety worries, and it does not fix the old ones either.
